metrics: Total residents, from survey responses collected 2020-2024 — the newest census data for these areas. Counts where people live: a business district's workers and a park's visitors don't count. Newer annual estimates exist for the city and its boroughs but not for these areas.
ACS population divided by land area: where people live, not how crowded a place is during the working day. The margin shown is the population's margin scaled by the same land area.
Square miles inside the City Planning boundary, clipped to the shoreline. Big parks, airports and cemeteries are separate areas and don't count toward any neighborhood here.
Half of residents are older, half younger. A survey estimate, not a count.
Residents younger than 18 as a share of all residents.
Residents 65 or older as a share of all residents.
Residents identifying as Hispanic or Latino of any race, using the census definition. Self-reported.
Residents identifying as white alone and not Hispanic. Self-reported; people choosing two or more races aren't in any single-race group.
Residents identifying as Black or African American alone and not Hispanic. Self-reported; people choosing two or more races aren't in any single-race group.
Residents identifying as Asian alone and not Hispanic. Self-reported; people choosing two or more races aren't in any single-race group.

Residents who were not U.S. citizens at birth, whatever their citizenship or legal status now; naturalized citizens count. People born abroad to American parents, and people born in Puerto Rico or another U.S. territory, were citizens at birth and count as native-born.
Speak a language other than English at home
Residents 5 and older who speak a language other than English at home. Says nothing about English ability — most also speak English.
Residents 5 and older who told the census they speak English less than 'very well.' Self-assessed.
People per occupied home. Excludes group quarters such as dorms, shelters and nursing homes.
Residents 15 and older who have never been married — including people in unmarried partnerships. Computed from the male and female counts in the census tables.
Civilian residents 18 and older who ever served on active duty. Excludes current active-duty personnel.
Civilian noninstitutionalized residents reporting at least one of six census disability types: hearing, vision, cognitive, ambulatory, self-care or independent living.
Lived in same home a year ago
Residents 1 and older living in the same home as a year earlier. Higher means less turnover; it says nothing about owning vs. renting.

Half of households earn more, half less. Households, not individuals. Computed from income brackets whose top bracket is $200,000-or-more, so the median caps there. Total money income from all sources — wages, self-employment, Social Security, retirement, public assistance and more — before taxes, excluding capital gains, in 2024 inflation-adjusted dollars.

Total money income divided by every resident, including children, in 2024 inflation-adjusted dollars. A few very high earners can pull it far above what a typical resident makes — compare with median household income.
Households with pre-tax money income of $200,000 or more in the past 12 months, in 2024 inflation-adjusted dollars.
Residents below the federal poverty threshold, which is the same nationwide — it does not adjust for New York City's cost of living, so local hardship is understated.
Residents under 18 below the federal poverty threshold (same nationwide standard, no local cost-of-living adjustment).
Households that received Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (food stamp) benefits at any point in the past 12 months.

Unemployed share of the civilian labor force — people without a job who are looking for one. People not seeking work (retirees, students, discouraged workers) count in neither the numerator nor the denominator.
Residents 16 and older who are working or looking for work. Retirees, full-time students and caregivers outside the workforce lower it — it is not an employment rate.
Residents 25 and older holding at least a bachelor's degree. Residents under 25 aren't in the base; students 25 and older are.
Residents 25 and older holding a master's, professional or doctoral degree.
Residents 25 and older without a high school diploma or equivalency.
Federal, state or local government employees as a share of employed civilian residents — where government workers live, not where government jobs are.
Residents working in their own unincorporated business, as a share of employed civilians. People whose own business is incorporated count as private employees instead.
Civilian noninstitutionalized residents with no health coverage of any kind — public or private.

Households with a broadband internet subscription: cable, fiber, DSL, satellite or a cellular data plan, which on its own qualifies. Dial-up alone doesn't count, and neither does internet access without a subscription.

What the middle renter household paying cash rent pays, counting rent plus utilities, in 2024 inflation-adjusted dollars. Households paying no cash rent aren't in the base. Reflects what current tenants actually pay — including long-held and regulated leases — not what a new apartment asks. Caps at $3,500 because of the data's top bracket.

Owners' own estimate of what their home would sell for, in 2024 inflation-adjusted dollars; half say more, half less. Not a record of actual sale prices. Caps at $2 million. Co-op owners estimate the value of their shares, which in limited-equity co-ops such as Co-op City sit far below market prices.
Renter-occupied share of occupied homes. The remainder are owner-occupied; vacant units aren't in the base.

Renter households paying 30% or more of household income on gross rent. The base leaves out renters whose share can't be computed: those paying no cash rent and those with zero or negative income. Includes the severely burdened.
Renter households paying 50% or more of household income on gross rent — a subset of the rent-burdened group, with the same base (renters whose share can be computed).

Residential evictions executed by city marshals in 2025, per 1,000 renter households. Only marshal executions count: tenants who leave after a court filing, a buyout or a rent increase never appear here, so this is not a measure of all displacement. About 6% of the year's evictions have no location and can't be placed. The count behind each rate is shown: where renters are few, a handful of evictions moves the rate a lot.
Homes in buildings built in 1939 or earlier, the census's oldest category.
Homes in buildings built in 2010 or later — a measure of recent construction, not of quality.
Homes in buildings with 20 or more units.
Homes that are one-unit houses, whether detached or attached rowhouses, as a share of all units.
Occupied homes with more than one person per room — the standard census crowding measure. Bathrooms don't count as rooms.
Half of homes have more rooms, half fewer. Rooms, not bedrooms — kitchens and living rooms count; bathrooms don't.
Units vacant when surveyed — for sale or rent, awaiting occupancy, seasonal or otherwise empty. Not a measure of abandonment or 'warehousing.'
Average one-way travel time to work for commuting workers 16 and older. People who work from home are excluded entirely.
Workers 16 and older whose main commute is subway, bus, rail or ferry. Each worker counts once, by their primary mode; people who work from home are in the base.
Workers 16 and older whose main commute is walking all the way. People who work from home are in the base.
Workers 16 and older who drive to work alone (carpooling counted separately). People who work from home are in the base.
Workers 16 and older who worked from home most of the reference week, as a share of all workers 16 and older.
Households with no cars, vans or trucks available to them.

Stations whose coordinates fall inside the boundary, each counted once by MTA station ID. Three stations appear twice in the MTA file under two stop codes (145 St, W 4 St-Wash Sq, Queensboro Plaza) and count once. Stations, not complexes: Times Square-42nd Street is five stations. Includes the 21 Staten Island Railway stations. A station just across a boundary street counts for the neighbor.
Police-reported motor vehicle crashes in 2025, placed by their reported coordinates, per 1,000 residents. Busy through-routes raise a neighborhood's rate; unreported fender-benders don't appear.
People hurt in crashes per 1,000 residents
People injured or killed in reported 2025 crashes — drivers, passengers, cyclists and pedestrians alike — per 1,000 residents, placed by the crash's reported coordinates.

Food establishments the Health Department has inspected at least once, per 1,000 residents; permit applicants not yet inspected are left out. Job centers score high because the denominator is residents, not visitors. The file can lag closures, so some recently closed places remain.
Standing live trees the Parks Department manages — street trees plus maintained park trees — per square mile. Natural woodland isn't inventoried tree by tree, so forested edges undercount.

Felonies reported to the NYPD in 2025, per 1,000 residents, placed by the coordinates NYPD publishes. NYPD records every rape and sex-crime complaint, and many offenses it couldn't geocode, at the precinct station house, so felonies at station-house points are left out: those points don't say where a crime happened. Complaints, not arrests or convictions. Job and entertainment centers rank high partly because workers and visitors are there but aren't counted as residents.
Murder, robbery and felony assault per 1,000 residents

2025 complaints for murder and non-negligent manslaughter, robbery or felony assault, per 1,000 residents, placed by NYPD's published coordinates, leaving out station-house points. Rape isn't included: NYPD publishes no incident location for it. Complaints, not convictions; other serious crimes like burglary are in the broader felony measure.
Every 311 service request over 12 months — noise, heat, potholes, parking and more — per 1,000 residents. Measures what residents report, which reflects reporting habits as much as conditions.

All 311 complaint types beginning with 'Noise' over 12 months, per 1,000 residents. Reports, not decibels, and one recorded location can supply most of a neighborhood's total: the board flags any location with a quarter or more of it, and 'Each location once' counts locations instead. A location is a geocoded point, not a verified building or caller.

311 rodent complaints (sightings and conditions) over 12 months, per 1,000 residents. Reports, not a rat census — attentive blocks can outscore infested ones. The board flags any single recorded location with a quarter or more of a neighborhood's total.

311 illegal-parking complaints over 12 months, per 1,000 residents. Reflects both parking behavior and neighbors' willingness to report it. The board flags any single recorded location with a quarter or more of a neighborhood's total.
